We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-409)
response:
Privacy amplification via subsampling is the mechanism by which differential privacy guarantees strengthen when a client participates in only a random subset of federated rounds — the intuition being that an adversary's uncertainty about whether a particular client's data influenced any given model update provides extra cover beyond the noise mechanism alone. The central question here is: under what conditions does this amplification break down when clients have heterogeneous data distributions and the aggregation rule is adaptive (e.g., weighted by loss, gradient norm, or cluster membership)? The core tension is that adaptive aggregation destroys the uniform subsampling assumption that amplification proofs depend on — if the server selects or up-weights clients whose updates are large or unusual, participation itself becomes correlated with data content, collapsing the privacy accounting. What a beginner misses is that the Rényi DP or (ε,δ)-DP guarantee they compute assuming i.i.d. uniform sampling can be vacuous in practice: heterogeneous distributions mean high-loss clients are systematically over-selected across rounds, effectively making their participation probability data-dependent, which standard amplification lemmas explicitly exclude. An expert worries about the compounding effect — each round of adaptive selection leaks a bit of distributional information, and over many rounds this can make the effective privacy loss grow nearly as fast as without amplification at all, even though the per-round noise looks adequate on paper.

The cleanest privacy-valid replacement is to decouple selection from data content entirely — either via uniform random subsampling (restoring the Poisson sampling assumption in Mironov et al.'s Rényi DP amplification lemma) or via shuffling-based protocols like those in the Google FLAME system, where a trusted or cryptographic shuffler anonymizes which client contributed which update before the server sees anything. A more practical middle path is instance-level privacy accounting with data-independent selection: Kairouz et al.'s 2021 "Practical and Private" paper shows that if you fix selection probabilities before observing any model state — essentially a predetermined round schedule per client — you recover amplification guarantees, but this requires committing to schedules that ignore current model loss, which directly sacrifices the convergence speed that adaptive weighting was buying. A third approach is per-client privacy budgets with composition tracking (used in Apple's deployments and studied in the DP-FTRL line from McMahan et al. 2022), where you simply accept that amplification is unavailable and instead tighten the per-round noise to hit a target ε without relying on subsampling credit — this typically requires 2–5× more Gaussian noise to achieve the same ε at the same δ, which in fine-tuning tasks translates to noticeable accuracy degradation at ε < 3. The utility cost is sharpest in the heterogeneous regime precisely where adaptive aggregation helps most: non-IID clients (e.g., Dirichlet α < 0.1 partitioning) can see 8–15% accuracy drops when switching from adaptive to uniform selection under matched privacy budgets in published FedAvg benchmarks. What experts rarely say plainly is that there is currently no construction that simultaneously achieves (a) amplification-level privacy accounting, (b) adaptive client selection, and (c) heterogeneous data — you must sacrifice at least one.

Uniform clipping and noising across all layers is almost certainly leaving utility on the table, and the evidence is now fairly direct: DP-Forward (Yu et al., 2022) and the DPText line of work both show that freezing lower layers entirely and applying DP only to the top transformer blocks or adapter modules can match full-model DP-SGD accuracy at roughly half the effective noise, because gradient signal-to-noise ratio is far worse in early layers where gradients are small and the sensitivity budget is wasted. The theoretical justification is that privacy cost under composition scales with the number of parameters being noised, not just the number of rounds — so concentrating noise on a smaller, task-relevant subspace (the last 2–4 layers, or a low-rank adapter like LoRA) reduces the per-coordinate noise needed to hit a given ε without changing the round count. DP-LoRA (Yu et al., 2021; also the BiomedLM fine-tuning experiments from Kerrigan et al.) demonstrates this concretely: fine-tuning only rank-8 LoRA adapters with DP achieves within 2–3% of non-private full fine-tuning on GLUE at ε=8, whereas uniform DP-SGD on all layers at the same ε loses 7–12% depending on task. The harder question is how to set per-layer clipping thresholds adaptively without spending privacy budget on the threshold-selection itself — AdaClip (Pichapati et al., 2019) proposes quantile-based adaptive clipping that is itself differentially private, but the quantile estimation eats roughly 10–20% of your round budget in practice. In federated settings the problem compounds because per-client gradient norms vary wildly across heterogeneous data, meaning a single global clip norm either over-clips minority clients (destroying their signal) or under-clips majority clients (inflating sensitivity and thus noise) — layer-wise per-client adaptive clipping is the right target but no deployed system does this cleanly yet.

The low-rank structure of LoRA adapters can increase membership inference risk relative to dense updates under a specific and underappreciated condition: when the rank is low enough that the adapter's column space is dominated by a small number of training examples, the singular vectors of the adapter matrix essentially fingerprint the data subspace, making it easier for an adversary to test whether a target example's representation lies within that subspace. Hayes et al. (2023) and related work on subspace membership inference show that for rank r << d, the effective "privacy surface" collapses — instead of needing to distinguish a target example's influence across d dimensions of gradient space, the adversary only needs to test alignment with r directions, reducing the hypothesis testing problem substantially and improving attack AUC by 5–15 percentage points over dense-update baselines at matched ε. The interaction with federated settings is worse because each client's LoRA update, being low-rank, is geometrically sparse in weight space — an aggregating server or passive adversary observing multiple rounds can perform singular value decomposition across client updates to identify which clients contributed dominant directions, effectively reconstructing data-correlated subspaces even after Gaussian noise addition if the signal-to-noise ratio in the top singular values exceeds roughly 1/√r. The practical implication is that the noise added to LoRA weights needs to account for this geometric concentration: the effective sensitivity of a rank-r adapter is not simply the Frobenius norm of the update but should be analyzed in terms of the spectral norm, which can be √r times larger, meaning standard DP accounting that uses Frobenius clipping under-estimates true privacy loss by a factor that grows with rank. Concretely, Yu et al.'s DP-LoRA experiments use Frobenius norm clipping throughout, which means their reported ε values are likely optimistic when an adversary exploits subspace structure rather than mounting a naive gradient reconstruction attack — the gap between reported and effective ε has not been formally closed in the published literature.

Standard DP with a trusted curator assumes the server adds noise honestly after seeing plaintext gradients — when the server is the adversary, this assumption collapses entirely, because the server sees each client's update before any aggregation occurs, making per-client gradient reconstruction attacks (like Zhu et al.'s DLG and its improvements by Geiping et al., which achieve near-perfect reconstruction from a single gradient at high resolution) trivially applicable without any cryptographic barrier. Secure aggregation (SecAgg, as deployed in Google's production FL and formalized by Bonawitz et al. 2017) closes the plaintext visibility gap by ensuring the server only sees the sum of client updates, never individual ones — but this is necessary and not sufficient, because an adversary controlling the aggregation can still learn from the aggregate whether a specific client participated, particularly in cross-silo settings where the number of clients is small (often 10–100 institutions) and each client's data distribution is distinctive enough that their directional influence on the aggregate is detectable. The correct threat model for a malicious-but-aggregation-constrained server requires verifiable aggregation plus local DP or input perturbation before SecAgg — meaning each client must add noise locally before secret-sharing their update, which is precisely the local DP model, but local DP requires noise roughly √n times larger than central DP to achieve the same ε, a cost that is devastating for fine-tuning where gradient signal is already weak. MASKCRYPT and the LightSecAgg line attempt to reduce SecAgg's communication overhead while maintaining aggregation privacy, but neither addresses the fundamental problem that a server observing aggregate updates over many rounds can run differencing attacks: if client A participates in rounds 1 and 2 but not round 3, subtracting aggregates isolates A's contribution with noise that decreases as 1/√(number of other clients), which in cross-silo settings with 10 clients gives essentially no amplification. The honest-but-curious cross-silo threat model therefore requires at minimum: SecAgg to prevent per-update inspection, local noise addition to bound single-round leakage, differential participation policies to prevent differencing, and ideally zero-knowledge proofs of update validity (as in ZКFL, Guo et al. 2022) to prevent the server from selectively excluding clients to amplify differencing — no deployed production system satisfies all four simultaneously.

Making participation oblivious transforms the threat model from "DP over gradient content" to something closer to anonymous communication, and the natural primitive is an oblivious aggregation protocol where the server learns only that some quorum of clients contributed, not which ones — this is precisely what Prio (Corrigan-Gibbs & Boneh, 2017) and its successor Prio+ achieve for aggregate statistics, and the ACORN protocol (Bell et al., 2023) extends this to federated learning by combining secret sharing with a shuffler layer that breaks the client-to-update linkage. The shuffler model is the most practical instantiation: clients send encrypted updates to an intermediate shuffler (either a trusted third party or a cryptographic shuffle via mix-nets), which permutes and forwards them to the server, so the server sees an unordered batch with no participation metadata — Erlingsson et al.'s amplification-by-shuffling result shows this recovers central-DP-level guarantees from local noise, with ε scaling as O(√(n·e^(ε_local))/n) rather than the flat ε_local of pure local DP, recovering roughly 10–100× tighter bounds depending on cohort size. The systems cost is substantial: mix-net shufflers require either a trusted intermediary (which relocates rather than eliminates the trust problem) or multi-party computation for the shuffle itself, and Verifiable Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (VOPRFs) or threshold blind signatures are needed to let clients prove eligibility for a round without revealing identity — Google's Boneh et al. anonymization work and Apple's Private Access Tokens use similar primitives for rate-limiting without identification, but neither is deployed in a federated training context. Auditability is the genuine tension: regulatory requirements (GDPR Article 5, HIPAA audit trails in cross-silo medical FL) typically demand that you can prove which institution contributed to a model, for liability and data provenance reasons — this is fundamentally in conflict with participation obliviousness, and the best current resolution is cryptographic commitments with delayed disclosure, where clients commit to a hash of their participation at round time, and the commitment is opened only under a threshold signature from a quorum of auditors, preserving obliviousness against the server while allowing post-hoc audits. The remaining hard problem is that even with oblivious participation, round timing is a side channel: in cross-silo settings, the latency pattern of aggregate updates arriving at the server leaks participation information with high confidence when institutions have characteristic network or compute profiles, and no cryptographic protocol addresses this without adding artificial delays that can double or triple round time in production deployments.

Timing leakage can in principle be folded into a DP framework by treating the timing channel as an additional output of a randomized mechanism — if the server observes a vector of arrival times (t₁, t₂, ..., tₙ) alongside aggregated updates, then participation privacy requires that this joint output be (ε,δ)-indistinguishable whether or not a target client participated, which means the timing distribution itself must satisfy the DP inequality, not just the gradient content. The formal requirement for "metric DP on timing" was sketched in Alvim et al.'s quantitative information flow framework and more operationally in Trojan timing attack analyses for mix-nets, where the key insight is that if client i's compute time is drawn from a distribution with mean μᵢ and variance σᵢ², then distinguishing participation requires the server to separate signal μᵢ from noise — adding Laplace or Gaussian delays calibrated to the sensitivity of the timing channel (roughly max|μᵢ - μⱼ| across clients) achieves timing DP, but this sensitivity can be 10–50 seconds in cross-silo medical FL where GPU heterogeneity is extreme. The practical requirement is therefore a two-channel noise budget: one ε_grad for gradient content and one ε_time for timing, with total privacy loss bounded by composition — but because timing and gradient content can be correlated (slow updates often mean large models or unusual data), naive composition double-counts, and the correct accounting requires joint mechanism analysis that treats (update, arrival time) as a single output space, which has not been worked out in the FL literature in deployable form. Dwork and Roth's original framework handles this in principle but gives vacuous bounds when timing variance is high relative to mean differences, which is common in practice; the tighter approach is to use Rényi DP composition on the joint channel, which Bell et al. (2023) gesture toward but do not fully instantiate for timing. The operational cost of genuine timing DP is that every client must sample a delay from a calibrated noise distribution before transmitting, meaning the slowest artificial delay in any round lower-bounds that round's wall-clock time — in a 50-client cross-silo setting with σ_delay calibrated to ε_time = 1, back-of-envelope calculations suggest median added latency of 30–90 seconds per round, which over hundreds of fine-tuning rounds compounds into days of additional training time and makes timing DP essentially incompatible with interactive or frequently updated deployments.

The honest answer is that the field currently treats each channel in isolation, and the total privacy loss across a realistic federated fine-tuning deployment is essentially unauditable — a system that reports ε=8 for gradient DP, separately claims participation obliviousness, and adds timing noise with no joint accounting has not demonstrated ε=8 end-to-end; it has demonstrated ε=8 for one attack surface while leaving the others informally bounded or unbounded. The fundamental obstacle is that joint mechanism analysis requires specifying a single output space that includes all observable channels simultaneously — (aggregated update, participation pattern, timing vector, round structure) — and computing sensitivity over that joint space, but the channels have different mathematical structures (L2-bounded vectors, discrete sets, continuous arrival times) that resist unified sensitivity analysis; the closest formal attempt is Pan-Privacy (Dwork et al., 2010), which bounds leakage across internal state transitions, but it was designed for streaming algorithms and has no direct instantiation for multi-round FL with adaptive components. Privacy Odometers and Filters (Rogers et al., 2016; Whitehouse et al., 2023) offer a compositional accounting framework that can track budget consumption adaptively across heterogeneous mechanisms, and the f-DP / GDP (Gaussian DP) framework from Dong, Roth & Su (2022) handles composition more tightly than (ε,δ) accounting — but both assume the analyst can enumerate and formalize every mechanism that touches private data, which in practice is impossible when timing, selection, and aggregation logic are implemented across different system layers by different teams. The closest thing to a coherent joint framework in deployment is Apple's differential privacy system, which uses a centralized privacy budget ledger tracking total ε across all data uses, but this works only because Apple controls the full stack and treats each feature as a named mechanism with pre-audited cost — cross-silo federated learning with independent institutions has no equivalent governance structure, making even approximate joint accounting a coordination problem as much as a mathematical one. The field's working assumption — that gradient DP dominates and other channels contribute negligible leakage — is an empirical bet that has never been formally validated, and given that participation metadata attacks in 10-client cross-silo settings can achieve membership inference AUC > 0.9 with zero gradient access, it is likely a bad bet in exactly the high-stakes domains (medical, financial) where federated learning is most motivated.
